Note-Taking

Most advice about note-taking is advice about procedure: draw this line down the page, use these abbreviations, follow this method. I am not going to tell you any of that, because I do not think it is the useful question.

The useful question is about outcomes. Your notes are not the point. What you can do with them later is the point. A system that works beautifully in the moment and leaves you with nothing usable in April is a bad system, however tidy it looked in January.

So: build whatever system you like. Here is what it has to be able to do.

Three Things Your Notes Have to Do

1. You can find things again

By the end of the semester you will have notes on several hundred pages of reading, a few dozen recorded lectures, and every class session. The test is not whether you wrote something down. The test is whether you can put your hand on it two months later without re-reading everything.

That means some kind of consistent structure: dates, session numbers, source names, headings — whatever lets you scan rather than hunt. It does not matter which. It matters that it is consistent, because an inconsistent system is one you have to read in full to search.

2. You can say where something came from

When you use a fact or an argument in an exercise, you need to be able to say where you got it: which source, and ideally where in it. A note that says peasants resisted conscription is worth much less than one that says peasants resisted conscription — Figes 61.

Build this in as you go. Reconstructing it afterwards is miserable, and it is the single most common reason a good point goes uncited (see the Writing Guidelines).

While you are at it, keep a visible line between what a source says and the exact words it uses. Mark direct quotations as quotations when you write them down, not later. Notes that blur the two are how accidental plagiarism happens, to careful people, years after the fact.

3. You can still open them in four years

This one sounds paranoid until it happens to you. Notes locked inside an app you stopped paying for, a platform that shut down, or an account you lost access to when you graduated are notes you no longer have.

Favor formats and places you control: a notebook you keep, plain text files, anything that exports. Be wary of scattering notes across half a dozen apps, which fails the first test as well as this one.

Choosing How to Capture

Different material deserves different treatment, and part of developing judgment is noticing which is which.

  • Memory alone. Genuinely fine for some things. Not for primary sources, numbers, or anything you will need to cite.
  • Handwriting, in a notebook or in the margins. Slower, which is the point: writing by hand forces you to compress and decide what matters, and that act of deciding is most of the learning. The trade-off is real, though — handwritten notes are not searchable, so lean harder on structure and dates to make up for it.
  • Typing. Fast and searchable, which makes it easy to transcribe instead of think. If you type, make yourself summarize rather than capture everything.
  • A mix, which is what most people land on: by hand in class, typed for readings, or the reverse.

There is no right answer here. There is only whether the result passes the three tests above.

A Note on Where Notes Live

A word-processing document is a reasonable place to write something and a poor place to keep things. Formatting matters enormously when you sit down to write an essay and not at all when you are taking notes, and searching across a pile of separate documents is harder than it should be.

If you want a system that will outlast this course, look into plain text or Markdown files: they are searchable by anything, open on any machine, and will still be readable long after this semester. That is a suggestion, not a requirement. For this course, a spiral notebook you actually use beats an elegant system you abandon in week three.

AI and Notes

Asking AI to summarize a reading is a legitimate way to orient yourself, and this course has no objection to it (see AI in This Course). But a summary you did not write is not a note. It records what a machine found salient, not what you noticed, and the noticing is the part that shows up in your work.

Use it to get your bearings before a close reading. Do not let it replace the reading.

Notes Checks

From time to time I will ask to see your notes in class, and doing so earns engagement points (see Grading Policies).

To be clear about what I am looking for: evidence that you have a system and are keeping it up. Not a particular format, not neatness, not volume. A messy notebook that is clearly being used every week is exactly what I want to see. Ten immaculate pages produced the night before are not.

This is also, frankly, a nudge. Developing a note-taking system you trust is one of the more durable things you will take out of a history course, and it is the sort of thing nobody gets around to without a reason.
